to be formed in clay, concrete, other material.
Condition: Where visible, they appear in good, reasonable, poor, defective condition.
Repairs should be undertaken where movement or deterioration is evident.
No repair required: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were
identified unless otherwise stated below. Routine maintenance appropriate to the age
of the hip tiles should be expected.
Repair hip tile: The covering along the slope of the roof structure (called the hip
tiles) is damaged or defective. This should be repaired soon, repaired now. The roof
covering may have to be disturbed to repair the flashing, and this can increase the
amount of the work. The owner of the neighbouring property may have some legal
rights over the shared chimney. You should check with your legal adviser before any
work is done.
Valley Gutters: The valley gutters are formed in lead, mortar, other material.
Condition: Where visible, they appear in good, reasonable, poor, blocked condition.
Blocked or defective valley gutters should be cleared, repaired, or replaced as necessary to
ensure effective drainage and prevent water penetration into the building.
No repair required: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were
identified unless otherwise stated below. Routine maintenance appropriate to the age
of the guttering should be expected.
Repair valley gutters: The valley gutter at the junction of the roofs to all, front, side,
rear, of the building is blocked, has loose mortar, poorly aligned. This should be
repaired soon, now. Adjacent parts of the roof covering may have to be disturbed to
repair the gutter, and this can increase the amount of repair work. This should be
repaired soon.

Repair verge: The mortar, tiles, slates, clips, caps, other items along the edge of the roof,
called the verge, are damaged, cracked, loose, other. This should be repaired soon and, if
significant, repaired promptly. Adjacent parts of the roof covering may have to be disturbed
to repair the verge, and this can increase the amount of repair work. This should be repaired
soon.
Repair Flat roof: The flat roof covering is weathered, blistered, split, torn, worn,
ponding, damaged, other.
Repairs or replacement should be undertaken before further deterioration results in water
penetration. To replace the covering, the work will have to meet the requirements of the
building regulations. This may increase the amount of repair work.
Causing damp – The observed defect is causing damp penetration to the building
below. The flat roof covering needs repair or replacement now. To do this, the work
will have to meet the requirements of the Building Regulations. This may increase the
amount of repair work.
Add text to: Section J1 - Risk to Building - The flat roof covering is weathered,
blistered, split, torn, worn, ponding, or defective and causing rainwater to penetrate
the building below.
Roof Spreading: The roof slopes to all, front, side, and rear of the building appear uneven
or undulating, and the adjoining wall appears distorted, cracked, bowing or leaning outwards.
These are visual indicators that may be consistent with roof spread and suggest that the roof
timber structure may require strengthening. I recommend that you instruct a suitably qualified
structural engineer or roofing specialist to carry out further investigation and advise on any
necessary remedial work without undue delay.
General maintenance: Roof coverings should be inspected periodically, particularly following
severe weather. Routine maintenance, including replacement of isolated defective coverings,
clearance of debris and localised repairs, should be expected throughout the life of the roof.
Add text to: Section J1 - Risk to Building - The roof slopes to the front, side and rear of the
building appear uneven or undulating, and the adjoining wall appears distorted, cracked,
bowing or leaning outwards.
If the Property is a Flat, add this: You should ask the management company whether any
repairs to the roof covering have been carried out previously or are currently proposed. Your
legal adviser should confirm responsibility for repairs to the roof covering with the
management company and ensure that an adequate sinking or reserve fund is in place to meet
the cost of future repairs or replacement, should the need arise. This may help reduce the risk
of unexpected repair costs or increases in the service charge.

entries.title: Rainwater Goods
entries.rawBlock:
Not Inspected: The rainwater goods could not be inspected due to access restrictions and the
height and configuration of the building. Consequently, I am unable to comment on their
composition or condition. As the roof is exposed to the weather, it should be inspected
regularly and maintained as necessary to identify and address any defects at an early stage.
Description: The rainwater goods comprise PVC, cast iron, aluminium, steel, concrete,
asbestos cement, other, gutters, downpipes, hoppers, and associated fittings.
Condition: Where visible, the rainwater goods appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, very
poor condition, consistent with their age and type. No parts of the rainwater installation were
dismantled or tested. The adequacy of underground drainage has not been assessed as part of
this inspection.
No repair required: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified
unless otherwise stated below. The rainwater goods appear to be adequately performing their
function. Routine maintenance appropriate to the age and type of the rainwater goods should
be expected.
Rainwater runoffs: Some rainwater pipes have not been connected to gullies or extended
sufficiently away from the building and allowed to drain directly to the ground. Rainwater
can penetrate nearby structures and potentially cause internal dampness, timber rot, or erosion
around the building. The discharge arrangement should be reviewed and improved where
appropriate.
Shared Rainwater Goods: The rainwater goods are believed to be shared with the adjoining
property. Your legal adviser should confirm ownership, maintenance responsibilities and any
rights or obligations affecting the shared installation.
If asbestos cement is selected, add: The rainwater goods contain asbestos cement. Because of
the possible asbestos content, you should get advice from a contractor experienced in this
type of work or an asbestos specialist before the pipes or gutters are disturbed in any way.
This includes activities such as cleaning out gutters, etc.
Repairs
Insufficient slope: The slope on the guttering is too shallow. This prevents the
rainwater from draining properly and may result in future leaks. The gutters should be
refitted with an adequate slope soon. You may have to replace parts of the system,
and this can increase the amount of repair work.
Damaged Sections: Sections of the gutters or downpipes are cracked, distorted,
broken, split, missing, other. This should be repaired soon, repaired now. Repairs
or replacement should be undertaken to maintain the weather resistance of the
building.
Leakage: Staining to fittings and adjoining elements and localised dampness indicate
previous or current leakage from the rainwater goods. The affected sections should be

checked for watertightness and repaired soon or repaired now, depending on the
severity of the defect. Repairs should be undertaken to prevent further deterioration of
adjacent building elements.
Blocked Gutters: Vegetation, moss, leaves, or other debris were observed within
sections of the guttering. The gutters should be cleared as part of routine maintenance
to maintain effective rainwater disposal.
Blocked Gullies: One or more drainage gullies serving the rainwater system appear
partially blocked, fully blocked. Blocked gullies may result in localised flooding
and water penetration to adjacent building elements. The gullies should be cleared and
maintained regularly.
Defective Connections: One or more gutter or downpipe joints and connections are
loose, missing, leaking, displaced, defective, other. This should be repaired soon,
now. Repairs should be undertaken to maintain the effectiveness of the rainwater
system.
Corrosion: Sections of the rainwater goods exhibit light, moderate, significant
corrosion. Corroded sections should be repaired or replaced where necessary to
maintain satisfactory performance. This should be repaired promptly if the damage is
significant.
Add text to: Section J1 - Risk to Building – One or more defects affecting the rainwater
gutters, downpipes, associated fittings, and drainage arrangements were noted.
General Maintenance: Rainwater goods should be inspected and cleared at regular intervals,
particularly during the autumn and following severe weather. Routine maintenance will assist
in preventing blockages, overflow, water penetration, and premature deterioration.
If the Property is a Flat, add this: You should ask the management company whether any
repairs to the rainwater goods have been carried out previously or are currently proposed.
Your legal adviser should confirm responsibility for repairs to the rainwater goods with the
management company and ensure that an adequate sinking or reserve fund is in place to meet
the cost of future repairs or replacement, should the need arise. This may help reduce the risk
of unexpected repair costs or increases in the service charge.
Condition rating 123

entries.title: Main Walls
entries.rawBlock:
The external walls have been inspected visually and by touch from the outside and internally
where exposed. No opening up or destructive investigation has been undertaken. The
composition of the wall material cannot be fully confirmed without causing damage to the
walls.
Description: The external walls of the main building, extension(s), other, are constructed
of (type 000) mm solid brick, cavity brick, cavity blockwork, timber frame, rendered
masonry, pebble dash masonry, other construction type(s).
Cladding: The external wall finish or cladding comprises facing brickwork, natural or
reconstituted stone, timber cladding, plastic panelling boards. weatherboarding, fibre
cement boards, uPVC cladding, fibre cement panels, composite cladding panels, glass
curtain walling, hanging tiles (including shingle or plain tiles), aluminium cladding
panels, terracotta cladding tiles, other finishes.
Condition: Where visible, the walls appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, very poor
condition, consistent with their age and type of construction.
No repair required: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified
unless otherwise stated below. The external walls appear to be adequately performing their
function. Routine maintenance appropriate to the age and construction of the building should
be expected.
Painted Walls: The external wall surfaces, or parts of them, have been painted. Painting
masonry can reduce its ability to breathe, trapping moisture within the wall. Rainwater may
penetrate through fine cracks in the paint but be unable to evaporate freely, increasing the risk
of dampness, frost damage and spalling of bricks or render over time. High internal humidity
can also contribute to moisture becoming trapped within the wall construction.
Painted external masonry also requires regular maintenance, as the finish will deteriorate and
require periodic preparation and repainting to maintain its weather resistance and appearance.
When future redecoration is undertaken, breathable masonry paint should be used where
appropriate to minimise the risk of moisture becoming trapped.
EWS1 Cladding: The external walls are partially or predominantly cladded with a brick-
slip, brick-effect outer face, rainscreen boards, terracotta tiles, compressed composite
boards, aluminium panels, glass reinforced concrete (GRC) panels, glass curtain
walling, hanging tiles (including shingle or plain tiles), aluminium cladding panels, etc.
This type of construction typically comprises fixing the cladding materials to a metal support
frame secured to the primary structure, with a ventilated cavity and non-combustible mineral
wool insulation behind. The inner leaf is commonly formed of concrete, blockwork or a metal
framing system incorporating sheathing board and plasterboard lining.
EWS1 form not required: Based on the visual evidence available during my
inspection, the external wall construction appears broadly consistent with a building
that may satisfy current EWS1 requirements. However, this inspection did not include
an assessment of the external wall system for fire safety compliance, and I am not
qualified to certify compliance.

Confirmation can only be provided following an assessment by a suitably qualified
fire safety professional, where required, and the issue of a valid EWS1 form. Your
legal adviser should make further enquiries of the seller or managing agent and obtain
a copy of any current EWS1 form, together with details of any planned, ongoing, or
completed fire safety or cladding remediation works before you exchange contracts or
commit to the purchase.
This inspection should not be relied upon as confirmation of compliance with current
fire safety legislation or lender requirements. Neither the surveyor nor this practice
accepts liability for any loss, costs or delays arising from the fire performance of the
external wall system, the absence or content of an EWS1 form, or any current or
future remediation works or associated costs.
EWS1 form required: The external wall construction observed during my inspection
indicates that a detailed assessment of the external wall system may be required to
confirm compliance with current fire safety requirements. My inspection was limited
to a visual assessment only and did not include opening up, intrusive investigations or
a fire safety appraisal of the cladding system.
Where required, confirmation of the fire performance of the external wall system can
only be provided by a suitably qualified fire safety professional following a detailed
assessment and, where applicable, the issue of a valid EWS1 form. Your legal adviser
should make further enquiries of the seller, freeholder or managing agent and obtain
copies of any current EWS1 form, fire risk assessments relating to the external wall
system, and details of any planned, ongoing or completed remediation works before
exchange of contracts or completion of the purchase.
Neither the surveyor nor this practice has assessed the external wall system for
compliance with fire safety legislation or lender requirements and accepts no liability
to you or any third party for any loss, delay, remediation costs or other financial
consequences arising directly or indirectly from the fire performance of the external
wall system, the requirement for or content of an EWS1 form, or any current or future
remedial works.
Minor subsidence: Diagonally stepped and other similar cracks were noted to the external
elevations of the property. Evidence of previous repairs, including localised repointing and
repairs to the bay and other wall sections, was also observed. Based on a single visual
inspection, it is not possible to confirm whether the movement is historic and stable or
whether it is progressive.
Although no significant distortion or evidence requiring immediate structural intervention
was apparent at the time of inspection, the cause, extent, and current activity of the movement
cannot be confirmed without further investigation and monitoring over time. You should ask
your legal adviser whether any guarantees, warranties, structural reports, or insurance claims
relating to these repairs are available. In the absence of satisfactory documentary evidence, I
recommend that the affected areas are inspected by a suitably qualified structural engineer,
who can advise whether any further investigation or monitoring is necessary before you
commit to the purchase.

Significant subsidence: Significant diagonally stepped and other similar cracks
associated with structural movement were noted to the building, the corresponding
internal walls, and the party walls. Where some of these cracks may have or have not
been repaired and the time of repair is unknown, I am unable to confirm, from a single
visual inspection, whether the movement is historic and stable or progressive. The
pattern of cracking is consistent with movement that may be associated with
subsidence or foundation movement.
I recommend that you instruct a suitably qualified structural engineer to investigate
the cause, extent, and current activity of the movement before you exchange
contracts. Your legal adviser should also establish whether there is any history of
subsidence, structural movement, underpinning, monitoring, insurance claims, or
structural repairs affecting the property.
If you proceed with the purchase without further investigation, you will be accepting
the risk that more significant structural defects and associated repair costs may
become apparent in the future.
Cavity Wall Insulation: There is evidence that cavity wall insulation has been installed.
Your legal adviser should verify the type of insulation used, the date of installation, and
whether any guarantees or warranties are available.
If it is confirmed that foam cavity wall insulation has been installed, please note that this type
of insulation has been associated with problems in some properties. These may include
deterioration of the insulation over time, allowing moisture to bridge the cavity and resulting
in internal dampness, or contributing to the accelerated corrosion of wall ties where
conditions are conducive. The availability of any guarantees or warranties should also be
confirmed.
Thin wall: The external wall to the front, rear, side walls of the main building, extension,
other is not thick enough and vulnerable to damp problems and heat loss. This substandard
construction should be improved soon. In some cases, rebuilding the wall to modern
standards may be the only economic option.
Damp-proof course: The walls have a barrier against dampness rising from the ground
(called a damp-proof course or DPC is visible, partially visible, not visible; one would
normally be expected for a property of this age and type. The DPC is assumed to consist of
plastic, felt, slates, engineering bricks, other. The adequacy of concealed damp-proof
courses cannot be confirmed during a visual inspection.
DPC Treatment noted: I noted evidence of damp proof course treatment, wall
ventilation apparatus, ventilation holes, other in the property. You should ask your
legal adviser to check whether there has been a dampness problem before and if a
valid guarantee or warranty covers this work.
If not, you should ask an appropriately qualified person to inspect the property, assess
its condition, and identify what repairs are required. Once the repairs have been
completed, this person should issue a certificate of ‘structural worthiness.’ You
should ask your insurance company if this problem would affect your ability to get
insurance cover for this property.

Moisture metre readings: Random moisture readings were taken to accessible internal wall
surfaces using a hand-held electronic moisture meter.
No damp found: No readings were obtained that suggest abnormal moisture levels at
the time of inspection.
Damp found: Elevated moisture readings were recorded to sections of the internal
wall surfaces that include (enter locations).
Penetrating damp cause: This may have been affected by penetrating damp
probably caused by overflowing gutter, roof leak, leaking downpipe, bridged
DPC, blocked gully, other. When the problem has been resolved, the wall may need
to be repaired.
Repair options: The source of the moisture should be identified and remedied as a
priority. This may involve repairs to the gutters, roof covering, downpipes, damp-
proof course, blocked gullies, damaged drainage, other, as appropriate. Once the
source of moisture has been eliminated and the affected walls have been allowed
sufficient time to dry naturally, any damaged plaster, decorations or other finishes
should be repaired or replaced, as necessary. The affected area should then be
monitored to ensure that the dampness does not recur.
Investigate cause: The source of moisture cannot be confirmed during a visual
inspection. You should instruct a suitably qualified contractor to investigate the cause
of the dampness and carry out any necessary repairs to prevent further moisture
penetration. Following completion of the repairs, the affected walls should be allowed
to dry before any replastering, redecoration or replacement of finishes is undertaken.
Premature redecoration may result in the recurrence of staining or damage if residual
moisture remains within the wall.
Rising damp: The wall(s) may be affected by rising damp. Probable causes include a
damaged, deteriorated or bridged damp-proof course (DPC), high external ground
levels, defective drainage, or other factors. The source of the moisture should be
identified and remedied by a suitably qualified contractor. Once the cause has been
addressed, any damaged plaster, decorations or other affected finishes may require
repair or replacement.
Add text to: Section J1 - Risk to Building – Elevated moisture readings and
associated defects to wall finishes were recorded on internal wall surfaces, suggesting
the presence of rising damp. Further investigation by a suitably qualified damp and
timber specialist is recommended to determine the cause and extent of the problem.
Install drain guttering: Because the external ground levels are high in relation to the
building, the damp-proof course (DPC) may be bridged in places, allowing moisture to
penetrate the walls. External ground levels should be reduced where practicable to maintain
an appropriate clearance below the damp-proof course. Where this is not feasible, suitable
drainage measures, such as a French drain or gravel-filled drainage channel, may be
appropriate to improve surface water drainage and reduce the risk of moisture penetration. A
suitably qualified contractor should advise on the most appropriate remedial solution.

Removed wall: An external wall to the lounge, kitchen, bedroom, other appears to have
been removed as part of previous alterations. This work should have been carried out with
Building Regulations approval and should have included adequate structural support for the
remaining wall above the openings. Due to the internal floor and ceiling finishes, I was
unable to confirm whether suitable structural support has been provided. I strongly
recommend that your legal adviser obtains confirmation that the necessary Building
Regulations approval was obtained for these alterations. If the required approval cannot be
confirmed, or the work was not properly supervised, there is a risk that additional structural
support may be required. This could result in further investigation, remedial works, additional
costs, and disruption.
Defect noted: I noted cracking, distortions, other in the surrounding wall surfaces.
However, due to the concealed nature of the structure behind the wall and the floor
and ceiling finishes, I was unable to confirm whether adequate structural support has
been provided. You should instruct a suitably qualified structural engineer to carry out
further investigation and advise on the adequacy of the structural alterations and any
remedial works that may be required.
Extensions and alterations: Evidence was noted that external alterations have been carried
out to the property. These include wall removal, new openings, replacement lintels,
structural alterations, building extension works, other alterations. Your legal adviser
should confirm that all appropriate statutory approvals and completion certificates have been
obtained where required.
No Structural Movement: Although I did not observe any evidence of significant structural
movement during my inspection, I cannot be categorical that none has occurred, as all
buildings are subject to some degree of movement, such as normal settlement and seasonal
thermal or moisture-related movement. It is also possible that evidence of movement,
including cracks, may be concealed by floor coverings, decorations, fitted furniture, or other
obstructions.
Normal defects: I noted no evidence of any significant recent or progressive
structural movement within the property. However, there are signs that the property
has experienced some historic movement, as evidenced by cracking to external and
internal wall surfaces, at junctions and around openings. As far as could be observed,
these cracks appear longstanding in nature, and there is no evidence to suggest
significant ongoing movement. No significant repairs are considered necessary at this
time, although localised repairs and redecoration may be required as part of routine
maintenance.
Recent defects: The front, side, rear walls of the main building, back addition,
extension, bay window, porch, other areas have been damaged by movement cracks
potentially arising from settlement, subsidence, nearby vegetation, point loading,
wall tie damage, other causes, and this is considered structurally significant.
Movement within the property is considered serious and could worsen over time.
Parts of the property could become unstable. You should instruct an appropriately
qualified structural engineer to investigate the problem and recommend an appropriate
scheme of repair. To carry out a proper investigation, it is likely that parts of the
property will need to be opened or disturbed, and this should be discussed with the

building owner. Evidence of previous structural movement, even where satisfactorily
resolved, may affect the property's future mortgageability and saleability.
Recurring defects:  The outside wall(s) to the main building, back addition,
extension, bay window, porch, other have been repaired, indicating that the building
has been affected by previous movement. However, recent cracking suggests that
movement may have recurred. This may indicate that the previous repairs have not
been fully effective. You should ask your legal adviser to establish whether any
guarantees, warranties or insurance-backed schemes are available in relation to these
repairs. If satisfactory information cannot be obtained, you should instruct an
appropriately qualified structural engineer to investigate the cause and extent of the
movement and recommend an appropriate scheme of repair. Evidence of previous
structural movement, even where satisfactorily resolved, may affect the property's
future mortgageability and saleability.
Differential Thermal Movement: Some of the observed cracking is consistent with
differential thermal settlement or movement between the replacement windows and
doors and the surrounding wall construction. This occurs because the varied materials
expand and contract at varying rates as temperatures change, resulting in minor
cracking around openings. The cracking appears longstanding and is not considered
indicative of significant structural movement.
Restraint steel rods: Lateral restraint steel rods have been installed to address
previous structural movement. Based on my visual inspection, the installation appears
longstanding, and I noted no evidence of recent or progressive movement associated
with the areas inspected. However, a visual inspection cannot confirm that all
movement has permanently ceased.
Where no recent cracks have been observed, this will indicate that the installation
appears to be performing its intended function, although its adequacy cannot be
confirmed without structural design information or intrusive investigation.
Trees: There are trees located close to the property. I noted no obvious signs to suggest that
they have caused significant damage to the property. However, it would be prudent to
implement a programme of management to control their future growth. Trees can affect
building foundations and below-ground services, particularly where shrinkable subsoils are
present.
Tree defects noted: There are trees located close to the property, and I noted defects
that may be associated with their influence, including cracking, distortion, heave,
other observed defects. Although the cause cannot be confirmed during a visual
inspection, further investigation by a suitably qualified structural engineer and, where
appropriate, an arboriculturist is recommended to establish whether the trees are
contributing to the observed defects and to advise on any necessary remedial works.
Spalled Brickwork: A few bricks exhibit minor, moderate, significant deterioration (this is
called spalling). Damaged bricks should be replaced where deterioration is sufficient to affect
the weather resistance of the wall.

Causing damp: This is allowing damp to get into the building. These should be
repaired now.
Repair pointing: The mortar between the bricks (known as the pointing) to parts of the
building is eroded, cracked, loose, missing, damaged, other. The defective pointing should
be renewed using a mortar appropriate to the age, type, and construction of the building. This
may comprise lime-based mortar or Portland cement mortar, as appropriate. Weathered or
defective pointing should be renewed as part of routine maintenance to help reduce water
penetration and minimise further deterioration.
Causing damp: This is allowing damp to get into the building. These should be
repaired now.
Repair render: Parts of the render coating to the building are cracked, eroded, loose,
missing, damaged. The defective pointing should be renewed using a mortar appropriate to
the age, type, and construction of the building. This may comprise lime-based mortar or
Portland cement mortar, as appropriate. Weathered or defective pointing should be renewed
as part of routine maintenance to help reduce water penetration and minimise further
deterioration.
Hazard: Rendering pieces are likely to fall and cause harm to people who may be
nearby. This is a hazard, and this repair should be carried out urgently.
Causing damp: This is allowing damp to get into the building. These should be
repaired now.
Wall Ties defects: Parts of the walls to the side of the property show evidence of previous
cavity wall tie repairs. No further repairs appear necessary based on my visual inspection, and
the property should be maintained in the normal way. You should ask your legal adviser to
confirm whether any guarantees, warranties or completion certificates are available for these
works. If satisfactory documentation is not available, you should instruct a suitably qualified
specialist to inspect the walls and confirm that the repairs remain satisfactory.
Repair defect: Some signs may be consistent with defective cavity wall ties.
Defective wall ties can affect the stability of cavity walls if left untreated. You should
instruct a suitably qualified specialist to conduct a detailed inspection, confirm the
condition of the wall ties, and recommend any necessary remedial works. Your legal
adviser should also establish whether any guarantees or warranties are available in
relation to previous repairs, if applicable.
Lintel defect: The lintel (the beam supporting the masonry above a door or window
opening), including a brick arch where applicable, in the front, side, rear, other wall of the
main building, back addition, extension, bay window, other is damaged, cracked, or
distorted.
Minor defects: The defects observed are limited and do not require significant repair.
Where appropriate, cracks should be filled, defective pointing repaired, and any
localised defects made good to help restore the integrity of the lintel or brick arch.
Repairs should be carried out in the near future to prevent further deterioration.

Significant defect: The defects observed are significant and have caused, or are likely
to cause, movement or damage to the adjoining masonry. Further investigation by a
suitably qualified contractor is recommended. Repairs may include repairing or
replacing the lintel or rebuilding the brick arch, together with making good the
surrounding masonry. The extent of the work required may increase once the lintel
has been exposed.
Add text to: Section J1 - Risk to Building – One or more small beams that span
across the top of the window or door opening, including brick arch (called a lintel), is
damaged, cracked, distorted.
Windowsill defect: The windowsill(s) to the front, side, rear, other wall of the main
building, back addition, extension, bay window, other is damaged, rotten, cracked,
distorted, other.
Minor Defect: Localised defects were observed. Repairs should be carried out to
prevent further deterioration and maintain effective weather protection.
Significant Defect: The windowsill(s) is significantly damaged or defective and may
be allowing water penetration into the building. Prompt repair or replacement by a
suitably qualified contractor is recommended. Associated repairs to the surrounding
masonry or window frame may also be required.
General Maintenance: External walls should be inspected periodically as part of routine
maintenance. Prompt repair of defective pointing, render, sealants, and isolated masonry
defects will assist in maintaining the weather resistance and structural integrity of the
building.
If the Property is a Flat, add this.
You should ask the management company whether any repairs to the external walls have
been carried out previously or are currently proposed. Your legal adviser should confirm
responsibility for repairs to the external walls with the management company and ensure that
an adequate sinking or reserve fund is in place to meet the cost of future repairs or
replacement, should the need arise. This may help reduce the risk of unexpected repair costs
or increases in the service charge.

entries.title: Windows
entries.rawBlock:
Not every part of the windows was inspected in detail. The inspection was limited to those
parts that were readily accessible without causing damage or moving furnishings. Only a
representative sample of accessible windows was opened and closed during the inspection.
Windows obscured by curtains, blinds, shutters, furniture, stored items, or fitted security
devices could not be fully inspected. Double-glazed units cannot be assessed for thermal
performance during a visual inspection.
Description: The windows are formed of replacement, original, old, PVCu, timber, old
style timber sash, modern PVC sash, modern timber sash, aluminium, composite, other
framed units.
Glazing: The glazing comprises single glazing, double glazing, triple glazing, secondary
glazing, decorative glazing, other.
No BS EN: No visible British Standard, BS EN, or other permanent safety markings were
identified on the accessible glazing. The absence of visible markings does not necessarily
indicate that safety glazing has not been installed. Where confirmation is required, your legal
adviser should verify any available certification relating to replacement windows.
BS EN noted: Visible British Standard, BS EN, or other permanent safety markings were
identified on the accessible glazing. The presence of visible markings indicates that safety
glazing has been installed. Where confirmation is required, your legal adviser should verify
any available certification relating to replacement windows.
Condition: Where visible and operated during the inspection, the windows appear in good,
reasonable, fair, poor, very poor condition, consistent with their age and type.
No defects noted: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were
identified unless otherwise stated below. Routine maintenance appropriate to the age
of window material should be expected.
If very poor is selected, add this: Windows that are in poor condition or in disrepair
will require comprehensive repair. In some cases, it may be more economical to
replace the windows entirely. This work should be done under an appropriate FENSA,
CERTASS, or Building Regulation approval scheme where applicable. Applicable
guarantees or warranties should be obtained.
If replacement window is selected, add this: The windows appear to have been fully
replaced or partially replaced. Where replacement windows have been installed, your
legal adviser should confirm that the installation was carried out under an appropriate
FENSA, CERTASS, or Building Regulation approval scheme where applicable. Any
available guarantees or warranties should also be obtained.
If old-style timber sash is selected, add this: Double-hung sash windows are
expensive to maintain and tend to be ill-fitting and allow heat loss. From time to time,
it is important to employ a joiner to inspect the sash windows, check the cords, and

ease them before redecoration. This is best done in conjunction with the redecoration
cycle.
Glazing seals: The external sealant around the window frames appears in good, reasonable,
fair, poor, very poor condition. Defective sealant should be renewed to reduce the risk of
water penetration.
Sill projection: Externally, the windowsills beyond the face of the walls appear to project
adequately beyond the face of the walls. The junctions between the window frames and the

roof access, limited lighting, health, and safety considerations.
Where roof space access was available, only those areas that could be inspected safely from
the access hatch and boarded areas were examined. Insulation, stored items, roof timbers, and
restricted headroom may have limited the inspection. Inaccessible areas have not been
inspected.
Roof Not Fully Inspected: I could not fully inspect the roof timber because of limited roof
height; the floor was not safe to walk on, floor was boarded, excessive storage,
insulation, underlining, other at the time of my inspection. No comments can be made
regarding unseen elements.
Unsafe floor: I could not fully inspect the roof timbers because the floor was unsafe to walk
on at the time of my inspection.

entries.title: Roof Structure
entries.rawBlock:
Loft converted: The original roof structure has been substantially altered to form the loft
conversion, with most structural elements now concealed from view. Consequently, I am
unable to comment on the condition of the concealed areas. Your legal advisers must verify
that all necessary planning permissions, Building Regulations approvals, and required interim
and final inspections were obtained for the conversion before you commit to the purchase.
The roof structure was inspected from the roof access hatch where available and from those
areas that were safely accessible at the time of the inspection.
Description: The roof structure is formed in traditional cut timber, prefabricated trussed
rafters, steel, other construction.
Condition: Where visible, the roof structure appears in good, reasonable, fair, poor, very
poor condition, consistent with its age and construction.
No defects noted: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified unless
otherwise stated below. Routine maintenance appropriate to the roof structure material should
be expected.
Roof Underlay
No Underlay: The absence of a roof underlay could result in water leakage, lower internal
temperatures, higher heating costs, condensation, and mould growth. I recommend that you
contact a qualified person to inspect the roof covering and confirm its watertightness.
Underlay present: The underside of the roof covering incorporates traditional bituminous
felt, breathable membrane, timber boards, other, which should provide a secondary
barrier to driving rain and snow, where visible.
Where visible, the underlay appears in good, reasonable, fair, poor, very poor
condition. Where no underlay is present, this is likely to reflect the age and type of
construction and is not necessarily a defect. However, installing a suitable breathable
underlay when the roof covering is next renewed would improve weather protection
and thermal performance.
No defects noted: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were
identified unless otherwise stated below. Routine maintenance appropriate to the
underlay material should be expected.
Defects noted: The roof underlay is worn, torn, missing, damaged in places,
reducing its effectiveness as a secondary barrier against wind-driven rain and dust. I
recommend that a qualified roofing contractor inspect the roof covering to confirm its
weathertightness and carry out any necessary repairs. Ongoing routine maintenance
appropriate to the roof covering should be expected.


Roof Ventilation
No ventilation: No ventilation has been provided in the roof space. The roof space must be
ventilated to the outside air to prevent dampness. When installing insulation, the ventilation
must not be obstructed.
Ventilation noted: The roof space appears to have adequate, limited, restricted ventilation.
Adequate roof space ventilation assists in reducing the risk of condensation and timber decay.
Where ventilation is limited, improvements should be considered when future roofing works
are undertaken.
Condensation noted: The roof space has no or insufficient ventilation, resulting in
condensation and mould growth on some of the timbers or roof underlay. Additional
ventilation should be provided to improve air circulation, reduce condensation, and
help maintain the condition of the roof timbers. Significantly damaged or rotted
timbers should be replaced.
Thermal Insulation: The roof space floor insulation appears adequate, limited,
insufficient, poorly fitted, other based upon the visible areas only. The thickness and
continuity of insulation cannot be confirmed without disturbing the insulation. Reference
should also be made to the Energy Performance Certificate where available.
Adequate insulation: The insulation to the loft floor appears adequate where visible.
Where insulation is inadequate or absent, you should upgrade it to a depth of 270–300
mm to meet current recommended standards, taking care not to obstruct roof
ventilation.
Inadequate/no insulation: The loft insulation is below the current recommended
standard of 270–300 mm or is absent. This can lead to heat loss, higher heating costs,
and an increased risk of condensation and mould. I recommend upgrading the
insulation to current standards, ensuring roof ventilation is not obstructed.
Water Storage Tanks: The roof space contains plastic, galvanised steel, asbestos cement,
fibreglass, other cold water storage tanks.
Condition: Where visible, the tank appears in good, reasonable, fair, poor, very poor
condition.
No defects noted: No evidence of leakage or significant defects was observed at the time of
inspection unless otherwise stated. Routine maintenance appropriate to the tank material
should be expected.
Leaking: The water tank is leaking or in disrepair. You should repair or replace this
promptly to prevent further dampness and damage to nearby elements.
Water Tank Insulation: The water tank and associated pipework appear adequately
insulated, partially insulated, uninsulated. Improving insulation may reduce the
risk of freezing and heat loss. The absence of, or inadequate, insulation could result in
condensation, dampness or leakage to the ceiling or surrounding areas.

Missing or Inadequate tank cover: The plastic, galvanised metal, asbestos, other
cold water tank cover(s) are missing or inadequate. This should be replaced soon.
Disused Water Tank: Plastic, galvanised steel, asbestos cement, other disused
water storage tank(s) remain within the roof space. Removal may be considered
during future maintenance where it is no longer required.
Timber defects: Localised distortion, splitting, cracking, notching, alterations, other
were observed. Repairs or further investigation should be undertaken where structural
adequacy is uncertain.
Timber Decay: Evidence of wet rot, dry rot, fungal decay, other timber decay was
observed. The source of moisture should be identified and promptly rectified before repairs
are undertaken. Ventilation to the roof space should be maintained to prevent conditions
favourable to rot.
Thin Timbers: Parts of the original timber structure are too small, and this could affect the
stability of the roof structure. You should ask an appropriately qualified person to inspect the
roof and recommend a repair scheme.
Heavy tiles sagging: The roof covering is too heavy and has caused the roof structure to
distort, sag, or cause nearby walls to crack. You should ask an appropriately qualified person
or roofing specialist to inspect the roof to determine the extent of the problem and specify any
necessary remedial works.
Spray foam insulation: Spray foam insulation has been applied to the underside of the roof,
fully or partially concealing the roof structure and preventing a full inspection of the roof
covering and timbers. Consequently, I am unable to assess the condition of the concealed
elements, and defects such as timber decay, wet rot, insect attack, or roof leaks may be
hidden.
Spray foam can restrict ventilation, trap moisture, and increase the risk of timber
deterioration. It may also adversely affect the property's mortgageability, insurability and
future saleability, as many lenders and insurers require specialist reports or removal of the
insulation before accepting the property.
Before committing to the purchase, you should: Obtain written confirmation from your
mortgage lender and insurer that the property is acceptable. Instruct an independent specialist
to carry out an intrusive inspection and advise whether the spray foam should be removed.
Ensure that necessary remedial works or removal are completed, or that the cost is reflected
in the purchase price. No opinion can be given on the condition of the concealed roof
structure, and I cannot accept responsibility for defects hidden by the spray foam insulation.
No Wood-boring: No visible evidence of active wood-boring insect infestation was observed
in the accessible roof timbers. Roof space is intrinsically a dusty place, and such evidence
may be concealed by dust and insulation. Historic flight holes may be present and are not
necessarily indicative of active infestation.

Wood Boring Noted: Evidence of active, historic wood-boring insect activity was
observed. Further inspection by an appropriately qualified timber specialist is
recommended where activity appears active or widespread. Otherwise, for historic
activity, further enquiries should be made to the vendor regarding its history,
treatment work, and guarantee certificates.
Roof Movement: Evidence of deflection, sagging, spread, other was observed. Observed
roof movement is normal, minor, significant, severe, presents a hazard, other. Further
investigation by an appropriately qualified roofing contractor is recommended where
movement appears significant or presents a hazard.
Structural Alterations: Evidence of structural alterations to the roof space was observed,
including loft conversion, altered roof members, removed struts, trimmed rafters,
replacement supports, additional timber supports, other alterations.
The adequacy of structural support cannot be confirmed during a visual inspection. Your
legal adviser should confirm that appropriate statutory approvals and completion certificates
were obtained where applicable.
Chimney Breast Alterations: Evidence was observed that a chimney breast has been
removed, partially removed, altered, rendered, other within the roof space.
Not inspected: Part of the chimney breast within the roof space has been removed. I
could not confirm whether the remaining masonry is adequately supported due to
limited visibility. Inadequate support can compromise the building's structural
stability. Your legal adviser should confirm that the necessary Building Regulations
approval was obtained. If this cannot be confirmed, or there is any doubt about the
adequacy of the support, you should instruct a suitably qualified professional to
inspect the remaining structure and provide recommendations before committing to
the purchase.
Adequate support: Part of the chimney breast within the roof space of this property
has been removed, and the remaining structure appears to be properly supported. Your
legal adviser should confirm that the necessary Building Regulations approval was
obtained for this work. If approval cannot be confirmed, you should instruct a suitably
qualified professional to inspect the structure and provide a report with any necessary
recommendations as soon as possible.
Poor support: Part of the chimney breast within the roof space of this property has
been removed, and the remaining structure does not appear to be properly supported.
Your legal adviser should confirm that the necessary Building Regulations approval
was obtained for this work. If approval cannot be confirmed, you should instruct a
suitably qualified professional to inspect the structure and provide a report with any
necessary recommendations as soon as possible.
Add text to: Section J1 - Risk to building - Part of the chimney breast within the
roof space of this property has been removed, and the remaining structure does not
appear to be properly supported.

Risk of collapse: Part of the chimney breast within the roof space has been removed,
and the remaining structure is not properly supported and is at risk of collapse. This is
a safety hazard. You should ask your legal adviser to check if the local authority gave
permission for this work. Further, you should instruct a suitably qualified professional
to inspect the structure and provide a report with any necessary recommendations as
soon as possible.
Add text to: Section J1 - Risk to building - Part of the chimney breast within the
roof space has been removed, and the remaining structure is not properly supported
and is at risk of collapse.
Add text to: Section I1 – Regulation - Part of the chimney breast within the roof
space has been removed, and the remaining structure is not properly supported and is
at risk of collapse.
Minor Chimney Damp: Minor dampness from water penetration was noted to the rendered
chimney breast within the roof space. This is not uncommon in a property of this age and
construction, as a damp-proof course would not normally have been provided to the chimney.
The moisture is likely to have been exacerbated by defects in the flashing where the roof
abuts the chimney stack. This is not considered a significant concern at present, but the
flashing should be inspected and repaired if necessary, during routine roof maintenance or
when the roof covering is next renewed.
Party Wall
Partially missing: The party wall within the roof space is incomplete, leaving gaps that
could allow fire to spread between this and the neighbouring property. The wall should be
extended to the underside of the roof covering and all gaps suitably fire-stopped as soon as
possible. As the party wall may be subject to legal rights and obligations under the Party Wall
etc. Act 1996, you should consult your legal adviser before arranging any works, particularly
where the proposed work may affect the adjoining property.
Largely missing: The party wall within the roof space is missing, creating a risk of
fire spread between this and the neighbouring property and reducing security between
the properties. The wall should be rebuilt to the underside of the roof covering and all
gaps appropriately fire-stopped without delay. As the party wall may be subject to
legal rights and obligations under the Party Wall etc. Act 1996, you should consult
your legal adviser before arranging any works, particularly where the proposed work
may affect the adjoining property.
Evidence of Water Penetration: Water staining or dampness was observed on roof timbers,
underlay, or adjacent structural elements. The source should be identified and repaired to
prevent further deterioration.
Capped Soil Vent Pipe: A capped soil and vent pipe was noted terminating within the roof
space. This arrangement is not considered appropriate, as any leakage or escape of foul gases
could discharge into the roof space. The pipe should be inspected by a suitably qualified
plumber to establish its purpose and condition. Where it forms part of the drainage ventilation
system, it should be appropriately extended and terminated to the outside air in accordance
with current requirements. Any redundant pipework should be removed or suitably sealed.

General Maintenance: Roof spaces should remain adequately ventilated and free from
unnecessary stored items that may restrict inspection or ventilation. Roof timbers should be
inspected whenever significant roofing works are undertaken. Prompt attention to water
penetration will reduce the risk of timber decay and associated structural deterioration.
If the Property is a Flat, add this.
You should ask the management company whether any repairs to the roof structure have been
carried out previously or are currently proposed. Your legal adviser should confirm
responsibility for repairs to the rainwater goods with the management company and ensure
that an adequate sinking or reserve fund is in place to meet the cost of future repairs or
replacement, should the need arise. This may help reduce the risk of unexpected repair costs
or increases in the service charge.
Condition rating 123

entries.title: Ceilings
entries.rawBlock:
The ceilings have been inspected from within the rooms only. No opening up or destructive
investigation has been undertaken.
Description: The ceilings are formed in plaster, plasterboard, lath and plaster, other
ceilings.
The ceiling finishes comprise painted, textured coating, papered, timber-clad, tiled,
wallpapered, decorative panelled, other finishes.
Condition: Where visible, the ceilings appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, very poor
condition, consistent with their age and construction.
No defects noted: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified unless
otherwise stated below. Routine maintenance appropriate to the ceiling material should be
expected.
If lath and plaster is selected, add this – The ceilings are fully or partially made of older
plaster supported on thin wooden strips (called ‘lath and plaster’), typical of properties built
before the 1940s. While no significant defects were noted at the time of inspection, these
ceilings can deteriorate with age as the plaster loses its bond with the timber laths. They are
susceptible to vibration and disturbance, and localised repairs are likely to be required over
time, particularly during redecoration or alteration works. Repairs can be difficult and may
dislodge adjacent plaster, making complete ceiling replacement more economical in some
cases.
If textured coating is selected, add this – Parts of the ceilings within the property may
contain asbestos-containing materials. In their current condition, these are not normally
considered a significant risk if left undisturbed. However, they should not be drilled, sanded,
cut, or otherwise disturbed without appropriate precautions. If future refurbishment or
replacement is planned, the material should be assessed beforehand and, if asbestos is
confirmed, removed by a licensed contractor. This can add significantly to the cost of future
works.
Minor cracking: Minor shrinkage or settlement cracking was observed in the ceiling
finishes. Such cracking is common in properties of this age and type and is not considered
structurally significant. The cracks may be adequately filled with appropriate material and
redecorated during routine maintenance.
Significant cracking: Significant cracking was observed in parts of the ceilings. Further
investigation is recommended where cracking appears progressive or is associated with
distortion.
Minor unevenness: Minor bowing, undulations, unevenness, other were noted on the
ceiling surfaces. These are not uncommon in properties of this age and do not necessarily
indicate structural movement.

Significant unevenness: Significant bowing, undulations, unevenness, other were noted
on the ceiling surfaces. Further investigation should be undertaken where structural
movement is suspected.
Wet water staining: Localised water staining was noted to the ceiling in the lounge, dining
room, bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, other. The moisture is suspected to originate from the
loft space, roof, bathroom, floor above, another concealed source. The source of the leak
should be identified and repaired before the affected ceilings are redecorated.
Dry water staining: Localised water staining was noted on the ceiling in the lounge, dining
room, bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, other. Damage consistent with previous water
penetration was observed. Although the affected area appears dry at the time of inspection,
repairs and redecoration should be undertaken as required.
Polystyrene Ceiling Tiles: Parts of the ceilings are covered with polystyrene tiles, which
present a fire safety risk. Polystyrene is highly flammable and, if ignited, can contribute to the
rapid spread of fire while releasing dense, toxic smoke and harmful fumes that can
significantly increase the risk to occupants. Although these tiles may have been acceptable
when installed, they no longer meet modern fire safety expectations. They should be removed
as soon as practicable by a competent contractor. Be aware that removal may damage the
underlying ceiling, particularly if the tiles have been firmly bonded, and repairs or complete
replacement of the ceiling finish may be required.
Heavy decorative covering: The ceilings are covered with heavy lining paper, decorative
finishes, or similar coverings. No significant defects were evident at the time of inspection;
however, these finishes can conceal minor cracking or other imperfections. Their removal
during future redecoration may damage the underlying plaster, and you should allow for
localised repairs or re-plastering.
Ornamental plaster repair: The ceiling incorporates ornamental plaster features, some of
which were found to be loose, cracked, damaged, unstable, partially missing, other. These
defects present a safety hazard, as sections may become detached and fall. A suitably
qualified plastering contractor should inspect the affected areas and carry out appropriate
repairs or replacement without delay. Localised repairs may be possible; however, where
deterioration is extensive, complete replacement of the affected ornamental plasterwork may
be necessary, resulting in more extensive and costly remedial works.
General Maintenance: Ceilings should be inspected periodically for signs of cracking,
distortion, or water penetration. Prompt repair of roof leaks, plumbing defects and
condensation problems will reduce the likelihood of damage to internal ceiling finishes.
Routine redecoration should be expected throughout the normal life of the property.
Condition rating 123

entries.title: Walls and Partitions
entries.rawBlock:
My inspection was limited by fixed furniture, kitchen units, bathroom fittings, large
appliances, stored items, tiled finishes, decorative wall coverings, and fitted cupboards, which
prevented full inspection of the concealed areas.
The condition of hidden wall construction, lintels, structural supports, and other concealed
elements could not be confirmed without opening the structure, which is outside the scope of
a Level 2 Home Survey. No comment can be made on the condition of these concealed areas,
and defects may exist that were not visible at the time of my inspection.
Description: The walls are formed in solid masonry, timber stud partitions, plasterboard
partitions, lath and plaster, other construction.
The wall finish comprises paint, plaster, wallpaper, tiling, timber panelling, textured
coating, decorative panelling, other finishes.
Condition: Where visible, the walls and partitions appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor,
very poor condition, consistent with their age and construction. Routine redecoration
appropriate to the age and condition of the property should be expected.
No defects noted: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified unless
otherwise stated below. Routine maintenance appropriate to the wall material should be
expected.
If lath and plaster is selected, add this – The walls are fully or partially made of older
plaster supported on thin wooden strips, called lath and plaster, typical of properties built
before the 1940s. While no significant defects were noted at the time of inspection, these
walls can deteriorate with age as the plaster loses its bond with the timber laths.
If textured coating is selected, add this – Some internal walls have a textured decorative
coating, which may contain small amounts of asbestos. If disturbed during repair,
refurbishment or removal, asbestos fibres could be released and present a health risk. Before
undertaking any work that may disturb the coating, you should consider having it assessed
and, if asbestos is confirmed or suspected, ensure any work is carried out by a suitably
competent contractor in accordance with current guidance.
Minor cracking: Minor shrinkage or settlement cracking was observed in the wall finishes.
Such cracking is common in properties of this age and type and is not considered structurally
significant. The cracks may be adequately filled with appropriate material and redecorated
during routine maintenance.
Significant cracking: Significant cracking was observed on some of the walls. Further
investigation is recommended where cracking appears progressive or is associated with
distortion.
Structural Movement: Evidence of historic, localised, progressive movement was
observed. Where movement appears progressive or structurally significant, further

investigation by an appropriately qualified structural engineer is recommended before legal
commitment.
Hollow Plaster: Localised areas of hollow-sounding plaster were noted. This usually
indicates that the plaster has lost adhesion to the underlying surface. Although stable at the
time of inspection, affected areas may become loose or detached over time. Localised repairs
may be possible; however, where deterioration is more extensive, or the plaster becomes
unstable, it may be more practical and cost-effective to remove and replace the affected
section. Repairs can be undertaken as part of routine maintenance or redecoration, as
necessary.
Condensation: Evidence of condensation and localised mould growth was observed on wall
surfaces, ceilings or window reveals, in the lounge, bedrooms, bathrooms, kitchens, other
area(s). Condensation is commonly associated with occupancy patterns, heating, insulation,
and ventilation. Maintaining a suitable balance between heating and ventilation should assist
in reducing condensation. Extractor fans may be installed, and windows opened regularly.
No Damp: Random moisture readings were taken to accessible wall surfaces using a hand-
held electronic moisture meter. No elevated moisture readings were recorded at the time of
inspection.
Penetrating damp noted: Elevated moisture readings were recorded to sections of
the wall surfaces including the (type wall location). Where there are built-in fitments
such as kitchen fittings, dampness can be difficult to trace but costly and inconvenient
to rectify.
Damp source known: Dampness was noted and is likely to result from defective
rainwater goods, blocked gullies, leaking pipework, bridged damp-proof course,
other. Where remedial action(s) have not been included in this report, it is
recommended that a suitably qualified damp specialist investigates the cause and
carries out any necessary repairs. This may require opening concealed areas, with the
owner's agreement. Associated remedial works may also be required, including
replacing damaged plaster and repairing or renewing decayed timber.
Repair Damp defect: The source of dampness should be addressed by repairing the
identified defects, which may include clearing rainwater goods, repairing defective
rainwater goods, unblocking gullies, repairing leaking pipework, removing any
bridging of the damp-proof course, other as appropriate. Once the source of
moisture has been eliminated, any affected internal finishes should be allowed to dry
thoroughly before being repaired or replaced. If dampness persists after these repairs,
further investigation by a suitably qualified damp and timber specialist should be
undertaken to identify any concealed defects and recommend any additional remedial
works. These repairs should be carried out promptly to minimise the risk of further
deterioration.
Unknown damp source: The source of moisture cannot be confirmed during a visual
inspection. Further investigation should be undertaken where moisture levels remain
elevated or visible dampness is present.

Suspected rising damp: Elevated moisture readings were recorded at the base of the
wall(s), consistent with possible rising damp, including the (type wall location).
Where fitted units, such as kitchen cabinets, conceal wall surfaces, the extent of
dampness cannot be fully assessed, and any necessary remedial works may be more
extensive and costly. I recommend further investigation by a suitably qualified damp
specialist to confirm the cause and advise on any necessary repairs.
Internal Alterations: Evidence was observed that an internal wall has been removed,
partially removed, altered, new opening created, has been formed. Where an internal wall
has been removed or altered, other parts of the property must be properly supported.
No defects noted: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified unless
otherwise stated below. Routine maintenance appropriate to the building material should be
expected.
Defects noted: An original internal wall has been removed to form an opening at (type in
location). Distortion, cracking, inadequate support, other issues were noted around the
altered area. While no significant progressive movement was evident at the time of
inspection, the structural adequacy of the alteration cannot be confirmed during a visual
inspection.
Your legal adviser should verify that Building Regulations approval and a completion
certificate were obtained for the work. If satisfactory documentation is unavailable, I
recommend further investigation by a suitably qualified structural engineer. This may require
opening parts of the structure, with the owner's agreement, to confirm that adequate support
has been provided.
General Maintenance: Internal walls should be inspected periodically for signs of cracking,
dampness, or movement. Minor cracking and decorative defects should be repaired during
routine maintenance. Maintaining adequate heating and ventilation will assist in reducing the
risk of condensation and mould growth.
Condition rating 123

entries.title: Floors
entries.rawBlock:
The condition of concealed floor timbers, floor voids, joists, sleeper walls, and foundations
cannot be confirmed without lifting floor finishes or opening the structure. Only the visible
performance of the floors was assessed during normal use.
The inspection was limited by fitted floor coverings, furniture, stored items, fixed kitchen
units, bathroom fittings, or restricted access. The floor construction has been inspected from
within the property only. Floor coverings were not lifted, and no opening up or destructive
investigation was undertaken.
Description: The floors are formed in solid concrete, suspended timber, beam and block,
other construction.
The floor finishes comprise floorboards, carpet, tiles, ceramic tiles, laminate flooring,
wood flooring, vinyl, stone tiles, other finishes.
Condition: Where visible, the floors appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, very poor
condition, consistent with their age and construction.
No defects noted: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified unless
otherwise stated below. Routine maintenance appropriate to the flooring material should be
expected.
No Creaking floor: I walked over the accessible suspended floor surfaces and found them to
be firm and level underfoot, with no evidence of excessive springiness or distortion. This is
based on a visual inspection only, and the condition of concealed floor timbers cannot be
confirmed without opening up the structure.
Creaking floor noted: I walked over the accessible suspended floor surfaces and found them
to be firm underfoot. Localised creaking and minor unevenness were noted in parts of the
floors and/or stairs. These are not uncommon in properties of this age, and, at the time of
inspection, there was no evidence of excessive springiness or significant distortion suggestive
of structural failure. This is associated with normal shrinkage or movement between
floorboards and joists. Repairs may be undertaken as part of routine maintenance.
Repair timber floor: The timber floor to the lounge, bedroom, kitchen, bathroom,
hallway, other is broken, poorly supported, uneven, springy, loose, sloping, incomplete,
damp, insect infested, rotten, poorly ventilated, others, and the defect(s) is considered
minor, significant. This is common with floors of this age and construction, and these should
be repaired soon. However, where the defect is significant, repair must be carried out
promptly by a qualified professional.
No Cracked Tiles: The floor tiles appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, very poor
condition. Where visible, the floor tiles in the kitchen, utility room, bathroom, toilet,
conservatory, porch, other areas showed no evidence of cracking at the time of my
inspection. No repairs are currently required. Routine maintenance only is recommended.

Cracked Tiles: Localised cracked, loose, damaged floor tiles to the kitchen, utility room,
bathroom, toilet, conservatory, porch, other areas were observed. Repairs should be
undertaken to maintain the floor finish and reduce the risk of further deterioration.
Loose Floorboards: Loose and creaking floor finishes were noted and will require local
repair or renewal. Removal of floor coverings may reveal additional defects requiring
attention.
Wood Boring Noted: Evidence of active, historic wood-boring insect activity was observed
in the property, lounge, bedrooms, bathrooms, kitchens, other areas. Further inspection
of active activity by an appropriately qualified timber specialist is recommended where
activity appears active or widespread. Otherwise, for historic activity, further enquiries
should be made to the vendor regarding history, treatment work, and guarantee certificates.
Timber decay noted: Decay was noted to the floor timbers, staircase timbers, bathroom
floor, kitchen floor, basement floor joists, other areas. The full extent of the decay could
not be determined during this visual inspection, and additional concealed defects may be
present. Further investigation by a suitably qualified timber specialist is recommended, and
you should obtain a report and quotations for any necessary remedial works before
committing to the purchase.
Dampness noted: Although I could not see the full extent of the dampness problem in the
lounge, bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, utility room, other areas, I suspect the dampness is
caused by faulty plumbing, bathtub spillage, leaking sealants, other. You should ask an
appropriately qualified person to inspect the floor and identify the full extent of the problems.
Unknown damp cause: Although I could not see the full extent of the damp problem, I
suspect more serious defects exist in hidden areas. You should ask an appropriately qualified
person to inspect the floor and identify the full extent of the problems.
Underfloor Ventilation:  Where applicable, the suspended timber floor is provided with
adequate, limited, or restricted underfloor ventilation. Adequate ventilation is important in
reducing the risk of condensation and timber decay. Where ventilation appears restricted or
limited, improvements should be considered during future maintenance works.
Laminate/Wood floor defects: The laminate or wood flooring to the lounge, bedroom,
kitchen, bathroom, utility room, hallway, other areas are worn, damaged, poorly fitted,
incomplete, cracked, lifted, other. These should be repaired or replaced soon.
Excessive floor vibration: The floor was found to vibrate excessively underfoot, suggesting
inadequate support and/or deterioration of the timber structure, such as fungal decay or wood-
boring insect attack. The exact cause could not be confirmed within the scope of this
inspection. You should instruct a suitably qualified contractor to inspect the floor structure,
including the underfloor void where accessible, determine the cause, and carry out any
necessary repairs before purchase commitment.
Sloping floor: The floor to the lounge, bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, utility room,
hallway, other rooms are slightly, significantly sloping. This is commonly associated with
long-standing settlement, historic movement, or deflection of the floor structure. Where the
slope is slight, and there is no evidence of ongoing movement or associated structural defects,

it is unlikely to be of structural significance, and no repairs are considered necessary. Where
the slope is significant, or accompanied by cracking or distortion, further investigation by a
suitably qualified building contractor is recommended to determine the cause and specify any
necessary remedial works before purchase commitment.
General Maintenance: Because floor coverings were not lifted, concealed defects may exist
that could not be identified during a visual inspection. No comment can therefore be made
regarding the condition of concealed floor timbers or supporting construction.
Floors should be inspected periodically for signs of movement, dampness, or deterioration.
Prompt repair of plumbing leaks, water penetration and defective ventilation will reduce the
risk of damage to concealed floor timbers. Floor finishes should be repaired or replaced as
part of normal property maintenance when they reach the end of their service life.
Condition rating 123

entries.title: Fireplaces, Chimney Breasts and Flues
entries.rawBlock:
This section relates to visible fireplaces, chimney breasts, and associated flues within the
property. The inspection was limited to a visual assessment only. Fireplaces, flues, and
appliances were not assessed, dismantled, or operated unless otherwise stated.
The internal condition of chimney flues, liners and concealed structural elements cannot be
confirmed during a visual inspection. No smoke testing, CCTV survey or opening up was

entries.rawBlock:
Trip Hazards: Potential trip hazards were identified, including uneven paving, damaged
steps, raised thresholds, uneven floor surfaces, loose floor coverings, damaged decking,
other. Repairs should be undertaken to reduce the risk of injury.
Damaged Stairs: The staircase requires some repairs based upon a visual inspection. Where
loose handrails, damaged balustrades or uneven treads are present, these should be repaired
promptly. Also, defective guarding should be repaired without delay.
Electrical Safety: Visible defects were identified. Further inspection by a qualified
electrician is recommended before legal commitment.
Gas Safety: Gas appliances and installations were not assessed. Where there is any doubt
regarding their age, condition or maintenance history, inspection by a Gas Safe registered
engineer is recommended before legal commitment.
Asbestos: Properties constructed before 2000 may contain asbestos-containing materials
(ACMs). As a precaution, we recommend that an asbestos identification survey is carried out
by a suitably qualified and licensed asbestos surveyor before purchase, particularly if you
intend to undertake refurbishment, alterations, or demolition works.
In addition to any asbestos-containing materials specifically referred to elsewhere in this
report, other concealed or inaccessible asbestos materials may also be present. The inspection
undertaken for this survey is not intended to identify or confirm the presence of asbestos.
According to the Health and Safety Executive (HSE), asbestos-containing materials do not
normally present a significant health risk if they are in good condition and remain
undisturbed. However, if such materials are damaged, drilled, cut, or otherwise disturbed,
asbestos fibres may be released, posing a health hazard and requiring specialist management
or removal.
Any work involving suspected asbestos-containing materials must comply with the **Control
of Asbestos Regulations 2012**. These regulations impose strict requirements on the
assessment, handling, removal, and disposal of asbestos, which can significantly increase the
cost of repair, maintenance, or alteration works.
If asbestos is suspected or confirmed, your legal adviser should make appropriate enquiries
regarding any previous asbestos surveys, removal works, or management records relating to
the property.
Further advice should be obtained where refurbishment is proposed.
Mould Growth: Localised mould growth associated with condensation was observed.
Maintaining adequate heating and ventilation should assist in reducing further mould growth.



General Advice: The inspection identified matters requiring repair, maintenance, or further
investigation. These should be considered before legal commitment and reflected in your
future maintenance planning.
Buildings require regular inspection and maintenance throughout their service life. Prompt
attention to isolated defects will normally reduce the likelihood of more extensive
deterioration and costly future repairs. Where specialist inspections have been recommended
within this report, these should be obtained before legal commitment where practicable.

K1 Valuations assumptions
Market Value: The opinion of market value reflects market conditions at the date of
inspection and valuation. In some locations, limited housing supply and strong buyer demand
may result in competitive bidding and prices above asking levels. Should market conditions
change, or the property's condition deteriorate, its resale value may be adversely affected.
Flats: Unless confirmed otherwise by your legal adviser, the valuation has been prepared on
the assumption that the property is held on a lease with an unexpired term of approximately
90 years and that there are no onerous lease terms or unusual liabilities that would adversely
affect its value.
Lease Length: The lease is assumed to have a satisfactory unexpired term, and no
immediate action is considered necessary. However, the value and marketability of leasehold
properties diminish as the lease term reduces. Once the unexpired term approaches or falls
below 80 years, the cost of extending the lease can increase significantly and the property's
value and mortgageability may be adversely affected. You should seek advice on extending
the lease well before it reaches this point. Your legal adviser should confirm the remaining
lease term and advise on any implications before you proceed with the purchase.
